solution_overview:
This problem describes the probabilities of a manufactured unit having one or more of three distinct defect types: Crack, Discoloration, and Warp. We are given individual defect probabilities, probabilities of pairs of defects occurring together, and the probability of all three defects occurring simultaneously. We will use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion and related set theory concepts to calculate probabilities for various combinations of these defects.

Let $C$ be the event that a unit has a Crack, $D$ be the event that a unit has Discoloration, and $W$ be the event that a unit has a Warp. We are provided with the following probabilities:

The probabilities of individual defects are:
$$P(C) = 0.18$$
$$P(D) = 0.22$$
$$P(W) = 0.15$$

The probabilities of units having two specific defects are:
$$P(C \cap D) = 0.06$$
$$P(C \cap W) = 0.05$$
$$P(D \cap W) = 0.04$$

The probability of units having all three defects is:
$$P(C \cap D \cap W) = 0.015$$

To address the statements, we will first calculate several key probabilities for compound events. The probability that a unit has at least one defect, $P(C \cup D \cup W)$, is found using the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion:
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = P(C) + P(D) + P(W) - (P(C \cap D) + P(C \cap W) + P(D \cap W)) + P(C \cap D \cap W)$$
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.18 + 0.22 + 0.15 - (0.06 + 0.05 + 0.04) + 0.015$$
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.55 - 0.15 + 0.015$$
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.415$$
This means the probability of a unit having at least one defect is $41.5\%$.

Next, we calculate the probability of having exactly two defect types. This involves summing the probabilities of pairwise intersections and subtracting three times the probability of the triple intersection, because the triple intersection is included in each of the three pairwise intersections.
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = P(C \cap D) + P(C \cap W) + P(D \cap W) - 3P(C \cap D \cap W)$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.06 + 0.05 + 0.04 - 3(0.015)$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.15 - 0.045$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.105$$
Thus, the probability of a unit having exactly two defect types is $10.5\%$.

The probability of having exactly one defect type can be derived by subtracting the probabilities of having exactly two and exactly three defects (which is $P(C \cap D \cap W)$) from the probability of having at least one defect.
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = P(C \cup D \cup W) - P(\text{exactly two}) - P(C \cap D \cap W)$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.415 - 0.105 - 0.015$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.295$$
Therefore, the probability of a unit having exactly one defect type is $29.5\%$.

Finally, the probability of a unit having no defects is the complement of having at least one defect.
$$P(\text{no defects}) = 1 - P(C \cup D \cup W)$$
$$P(\text{no defects}) = 1 - 0.415$$
$$P(\text{no defects}) = 0.585$$
So, the probability of a unit having no defects is $58.5\%$. These calculated probabilities will be used to evaluate the statements.

$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = P(C) + P(D) + P(W) - (P(C \cap D) + P(C \cap W) + P(D \cap W)) + P(C \cap D \cap W)$$
Substituting the given values:
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.18 + 0.22 + 0.15 - (0.06 + 0.05 + 0.04) + 0.015$$

$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.415$$
As a percentage, this is $41.5\%$. The statement claims this probability is above $43\%$. Since $41.5\% \not> 43\%$, the statement is False.

This statement requests the probability that a unit has exactly one defect type. This probability, $P(\text{exactly one})$, was derived in the overview using the sum of $P(C \cup D \cup W)$ and the probabilities of having exactly two and exactly three defects:
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = P(C \cup D \cup W) - P(\text{exactly two}) - P(C \cap D \cap W)$$
Using the values calculated in the overview:
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.415 - 0.105 - 0.015$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.295$$
Expressed as a percentage, this is $29.5\%$. The claim asserts that this probability exceeds $30\%$. Since $29.5\% \not> 30\%$, the statement is False.

**C.** → True

This statement asks for the probability that the unit has exactly two defect types. This probability, $P(\text{exactly two})$, is calculated by summing the probabilities of the pairwise intersections and subtracting three times the probability of the triple intersection, as the triple intersection is counted in each pair:
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = P(C \cap D) + P(C \cap W) + P(D \cap W) - 3P(C \cap D \cap W)$$
Substituting the given values:
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.06 + 0.05 + 0.04 - 3(0.015)$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.15 - 0.045$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.105$$
As a percentage, this is $10.5\%$. The claim states this probability is at least $10\%$. Since $10.5\% \ge 10\%$, the statement is True.

**D.** → False

This statement concerns the probability that a unit has no defects. This is the complement of the event that a unit has at least one defect, $P(C \cup D \cup W)$. The probability of having no defects is $1 - P(C \cup D \cup W)$.
From the overview, the probability of having at least one defect is:
$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.415$$
So, the probability of having no defects is:
$$P(\text{no defects}) = 1 - 0.415$$
$$P(\text{no defects}) = 0.585$$
Expressed as a percentage, this is $58.5\%$. The claim states this probability is under $58\%$. Since $58.5\% \not< 58\%$, the statement is False.

**E.** → True

This statement asks for the probability that the unit has at least two defect types. This event can be expressed as the sum of the probability of having exactly two defect types and the probability of having exactly three defect types.
The probability of having exactly two defect types, $P(\text{exactly two})$, was calculated in the overview:
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.105$$
The probability of having exactly three defect types is given directly in the problem context:
$$P(C \cap D \cap W) = 0.015$$
Therefore, the probability of having at least two defect types is:
$$P(\text{at least two}) = P(\text{exactly two}) + P(C \cap D \cap W)$$
$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.105 + 0.015$$
$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.120$$
As a percentage, this is $12.0\%$. The claim states this probability is under $13\%$. Since $12.0\% < 13\%$, the statement is True.
